01

Installation & line configuration

CAL = Cellular Automation Line. The bench-top configuration is built from three modules joined by a sample-rack track: SC-120 slide maker & stainer plus two CBC/DIFF analyzers of the same model — CAL 6000 = BC-6200 ×2 + SC-120 + Track, or the BC-6000 equivalent. A larger CAL 8000 line exists for higher-volume core labs (>400 samples/day); CAL 6000 targets 200–500 samples/day.

Both analyzer bays and the SC-120 have independent loading and unloading platforms: the BC-6000/6200 bays each hold up to 100 sample tubes, the SC-120 loading area holds up to 70, and the shared unloading platform holds up to 100. Racks can be dropped on any loading platform — the line's workload software (CMU) decides which analyzer bay picks up each rack.

Two-way loading lets racks be fed from either end of the track, so both analyzer bays stay evenly loaded instead of queuing behind a single feed point.

Fig. 1 — CAL 6000 module layout, read right → left: ① Loading → ② / ③ BC-6200 ×2 (CBC+DIFF) → ④ SC-120 (smear, flagged samples only) → ⑤ Unloading.

Reservation & scheduled startup

The line can be set to power on ~20 minutes ahead of the first shift so fluidics initialization and background checks are already complete when staff arrive. Reservation covers analysis windows, QC time, reagent replacement and print scheduling per day of week — configured once per line rather than per analyzer.

02

How the line operates

CMU — workload orchestration

The Central Management Unit balances load between the two analyzer bays and the SC-120, decides which samples need a blood smear, and surfaces reagent levels and unit status for every module on one screen — the operator works one queue, not three instruments.

STAT priority — cap-piercing

An urgent sample doesn't wait behind the queue: pressing STAT opens a dedicated loading slot, the tube is pierced and analyzed immediately, and the line resumes the routine queue afterward.

Multi-"R" — automatic reflex logic

  • Repeat — re-runs the same test after a system-level error, no clinical reason.
  • Rerun — keeps the first result but reruns in the same mode when a result looks suspect.
  • Reflex — automatically adds a test (e.g. RET, PLT-O) when a parameter is flagged.
  • Re-exam — routes the tube to the SC-120 for a smear when it meets the site's re-exam criteria (result, age, sex, department, time…).

Because criteria are configurable per site, the line can be tuned to minimize unnecessary smears without missing clinically significant ones — this is the lever most worth revisiting after go-live.

Fig. 2 — Multi-"R" decision path from a completed CBC+DIFF result to the next automatic action.
03

LabXpert — validation & TAT rules

LabXpert is the line's rule engine for autoverification. Every result is checked against a stack of pre-defined rules before it either publishes automatically or is routed for manual review — this is what turns "220 tests/hour" into results a tech doesn't have to eyeball one by one.

Fig. 3 — LabXpert autoverification stack: any rule that fails sends the sample to grey-zone / manual review or triggers re-exam; a sample that clears every rule passes automatically.

Rule categories

Critical valueParameter/flag combinations needing immediate call-out
Abnormal-range deltaChange vs. the patient's history outside abnormal-range tolerance
Normal-range deltaChange vs. history outside normal-range tolerance
Clinical exceptionSite-defined conditions (diagnosis, ward, therapy) that override default logic
Manual review conditionAnything else the site flags for a human look before release

TAT alarm setup

Two independent clocks run from a configurable starting event (e.g. tube loaded):

  • TAT warning time — first, softer alert that a sample is running long
  • TAT timeout — hard alarm that the turnaround SLA has been breached

Both are set per test panel (CBC, CDR, CD, RET…), so a STAT panel and a routine CBC can carry different clocks on the same line.

04

Line-level upkeep

Reagent workbench

All bulk reagents live in a customized cabinet under the instruments; fluorescent dyes are changed from the front cover without pulling an analyzer out of the line.

ECO mode

Any analyzer bay can be powered down independently; the SC-120 has an ECO idle mode that cuts reagent and electricity use without a full shutdown/restart cycle.

Usage-based service

Maintenance on the line is generally triggered by sample/slide counts and run hours, not the calendar — see each module's own maintenance table for exact thresholds.

Field note. Because CAL 6000 pools two analyzers behind one queue, a single bay can be taken down for maintenance or an error without stopping the line — the CMU keeps routing to the remaining bay and the SC-120. Confirm this fail-over behavior with the site during commissioning so it's documented in their SOP.

02

Operating principle — five channels, three technologies

Every CBC+DIFF result is assembled from five counting channels, each pairing a physical measurement principle with a specific reagent chemistry:

ChannelTechnologyReagentsYields
DIFFLaser scatter + fluorescence (SF-Cube)LD Lyse / FD DyeNEU, LYM, MON, EOS, IMG
WNB (BC-6000/6200) / BASO+NRBC (BC-6800)Laser scatter + fluorescenceLN Lyse / FN DyeWBC, BASO, NRBC
RET (BC-6200 only)Sphering + laser scatter + fluorescenceDR Diluent / FR DyeRET, IRF, LFR/MFR/HFR, RHE
RBC / PLTDC (electrical) impedanceDS DiluentRBC, PLT, MCV, MPV, histograms
HGBColorimetry (Lambert-Beer)LH LyseHGB
Fig. 4 — SF-Cube: one flow-cell measurement yields three independent axes (S / S / F) at once, instead of three separate passes.

SF-Cube optics (DIFF / WNB / RET)

A single cell crossing the laser beam produces three simultaneous signals:

  • Forward scatter (S) → cell size
  • Side scatter (S) → internal complexity / granularity
  • Fluorescence (F) → DNA/RNA content, from the fluorescent dye binding nucleic acids

Plotting all three gives a 3-D scattergram where each leukocyte population — neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, immature granulocytes, blasts/atypical lymphocytes — separates into its own cluster by size, granularity and nuclear fluorescence together, rather than by any single axis.

RET channel — sphering first

Reticulocytes only stain reliably once they're forced into a uniform round shape (sphering, via DR diluent) — an unsphered cell scatters light differently depending on which face hits the laser, corrupting the size/complexity signal. After sphering, FR dye binds residual RNA, and fluorescence intensity separates reticulocytes into LFR / MFR / HFR fractions (low/medium/high fluorescence — the ICSH's four reticulocyte maturity types collapse into these three reportable bands).

RBC / PLT — DC impedance

A cell passing through a small aperture under vacuum, between two electrodes carrying a constant current, momentarily raises the electrical resistance. The resulting voltage pulse is proportional to cell volume — pulse height sorts red cells and platelets by size into the RBC and PLT histograms.

HGB — colorimetry

Per the Lambert-Beer law, absorbance of a monochromatic beam through the lysed, HGB-reagent-treated sample is proportional to hemoglobin concentration — a larger photo-detector and stronger lyse reduce interference from high WBC counts and lipemic samples versus older, smaller-detector designs.

RBC histogram — shape, cutoffs, flags

The RBC impedance histogram plots cell count against volume (fL). A healthy sample gives one smooth, roughly Gaussian peak; the analyzer applies two fixed volume cutoffs to bucket the tails and watches the whole curve's shape for two distinct fault patterns:

  • 60 fL — cells smaller than this are counted toward Micro%* (microcyte fraction)
  • 120 fL — cells larger than this are counted toward Macro%* (macrocyte fraction)
  • RBC Abn Hist flags when the distribution departs from normality (skewed, flattened, or cut off at either edge)
  • Dimorphic Population flags when the histogram shows more than one peak — e.g. a transfused patient carrying both their own and donor RBC populations, or combined iron-deficiency/B12-deficiency anemia

PLT histogram — shape, cutoffs, flags

The PLT impedance histogram sits at the small-volume end of the same size axis, immediately adjacent to the red-cell curve — so most PLT flagging logic is really about whether the analyzer can tell the two populations apart at their shared boundary:

FlagCriterionWhat it means
Thrombocytopenia / ThrombocytosisPLT < 60 / > 600 ×10⁹/LDefinitive count-based flag, no histogram shape involved.
PLT Abn HistPLT-UP > 33%Too much curve mass sits at the upper (large-platelet) end — the PLT/RBC discriminator can't cleanly separate the two populations, so the count is suspect.
PLT Clumps?PLT > 50 & MPV > 13 fL & PLT-UP > 33%Large apparent platelets plus a heavy upper tail — classic signature of platelet aggregates being counted as oversized single platelets. Corroborated by extra events in the DIFF, RET, and NRBC scattergrams.
Large platelets (P-LCR)P-LCR > 12 fL cutoffP-LCR (platelet-large cell ratio) reports the fraction of platelets above a fixed large-cell cutoff; feeds P-LCC = PLT × P-LCR.
Reading the two histograms together. When PLT Abn Hist and PLT Clumps? both fire alongside an unexpectedly low PLT-I, check the smear before releasing the count — PLT-O (optical) is the first fallback, and if that is also unreliable the result should be flagged invalid rather than reported (see PLT-O vs PLT-I below).

PLT-O vs PLT-I. PLT-I (impedance) is reported by default; when RBC fragments, giant platelets, or platelet clumps make the impedance count unreliable, the analyzer falls back to PLT-O (optical + fluorescence), which is far less sensitive to these interferences. If neither is reliable, PLT is flagged invalid and a manual/microscopic count is required.

Buffer consumption — a real number worth planning around

Per Mindray's own competitive comparison, 5 L of Buffer reagent stains ≈ 925 slides on the SC-120 — versus ≈139 slides on a competing stainer (SP-50) consuming the same 5 L, a ~7× difference. Useful for estimating buffer reorder cadence against a site's actual slide volume.

Consumables & slide baskets

Blank slides load into the right-panel chute — up to 150 at once, oriented logo-up, topped up two boxes (100 slides) at a time when the low-slide alarm fires. Finished baskets push out automatically once they hold 10 slides (or fewer, if none are still processing); "Reclaim Now" can pull a basket early, but the slides inside may not be fully dry yet. The unloading area alarms below 3 baskets on hand. Reagents (diluent, probe cleanser, stain/buffer/methanol) sit in the cabinet beneath the unit.

02

How a slide gets made and stained

Fig. 5 — Slide-making workflow: sample-preparation steps (aspirate/detect) feed directly into the mechanical smearing sequence.

Viscosity-adaptive smearing

Rather than one fixed protocol, the SC-120 measures each sample's viscosity and selects from 19 pre-set protocols, each tuning blood-dispense volume, spreader pull/push angle, pull/push speed, and dwell time. A high-HCT (viscous) sample gets a smaller drop, gentler angle and slower push; a low-HCT sample gets more blood, a larger angle and faster push — mirroring what an experienced tech adjusts by feel.

Staining cycle — 4 positions

Fig. 6 — Staining protocol with methanol pre-fixation: a slide advances through four fixed positions per cycle.

Romanowsky stain chemistry

All seven SC-120 protocols are Romanowsky-type stains (methylene blue / azure B + eosin), reacting with cell components at pH 6.4–7.0:

  • Basic (acidophilic) particles bind eosin → red — hemoglobin, eosinophil granules
  • Acidic (basophilic) particles bind methylene blue → blue/purple — lymphocyte cytoplasm, basophil granules
  • Neutral particles bind both, isoelectric → light purple-red
  • Nucleus (DNA + basic histones) → purple-red, dominated by the weaker blue reaction

Methanol pre-fixation dehydrates and fixes the cell before staining, increasing surface area for stain uptake and giving noticeably better RBC morphology than staining without a pre-fix step — reagent-grade (>99.5% purity) methanol matters here; substituting ethanol measurably weakens the fix.

7 staining protocols (Menu → Setup → Stain)

  • Wright's Stain — with / without Methanol Prefix
  • Wright's-Giemsa Stain — with / without Methanol Prefix
  • May-Giemsa Stain — with / without Methanol Prefix
  • Liu Stain

One radio-button selection sets the protocol currently in use system-wide; only one protocol runs at a time.

Heating & drying settings

Where it lives physically

The heating core, drive boards and cooling fans sit together in the main-unit electronics bay, accessed from the side panel during FRU-level service — 3 fans keep the slide-drying zone's airflow stable.

ParameterRecommended valueWhere to check it
Blood-film drying target≈ 25 °CService → Status → Temp.&Humidity&Pressure
Heating-core target≈ 45 °CService → Status → Temp.&Humidity&Pressure
Drying fan cutoffstops < 40 °CService → Status → Temp.&Humidity&Pressure (2nd page — fan rotation speed)
Intermittent drying interval≈ 4.1 s (default)Setup → Stain / Service-level tuning
Under- vs. over-drying. Under-drying deforms RBC morphology on the finished smear; over-drying can trip the unit's own thermal/timing checks. Half-year service inspection includes confirming all displayed temperature, humidity and pressure/vacuum values sit in range, and that the 3 drying fans reach stable rotation speed within 5–10 minutes of a status check.

Moderate / slightly-thick / thick / thin / slightly-thin, and ±5 / 10 / 15% length trims — administrator-level; finer service-level tuning is engineer-gated.

Drying

Recommended blood-film drying target ≈ 25 °C, heating-core target ≈ 45 °C (fan stops below ≈ 40 °C); intermittent drying ≈ 4.1 s is the vendor-recommended default — under-drying deforms RBCs, over-drying can fault the unit.

Troubleshooting & field case

Selected errors

Voltage abnormal
  1. Power off and restart after a short wait.
  2. If it persists, contact Mindray service.
Diluent expired
  1. Tap Remove Error — a replace-reagent prompt appears.
  2. Replace the reagent; error clears automatically.
  3. If it persists, contact service.
Piercing mechanism not at expected position
  1. Tap Remove Error — the system attempts self-recovery.
  2. If it persists, contact service (mechanical inspection likely needed).
Barcode not read
  1. Confirm the label is affixed correctly and undamaged.
  2. If labels routinely can't meet spec, barcode scanning can be disabled per-site.

Consumable menu — Flow Rate & Fluid Volume tests

This is almost certainly what an earlier revision of this guide called the "4/8 cuvette test" — the actual screen lives under the toolbar's Consumable tab, and the units at stake are the staining cassettes/boxes (7 of them), not cuvettes. Two independent self-tests live here:

Flow Rate Test

Spreader Slide Air Drying Flow Rate Test
Spreader Slide Cleaning Fluid Rate Test

Fluid Volume Test

Injection Volume Test (7 cassettes)
Residual Volume Test (4 cassettes)

Injection Volume Test — what each of the 7 boxes should read

Running this test dispenses each dispensing pump's (DP1–DP6) fluid into its own staining box/cassette and outputs all 7 side by side — a quick visual + volumetric check that every pump is delivering its nominal amount, rather than inferring it indirectly from stain quality on a finished slide:

Box #LiquidSource pumpExpected volume
1DI WaterDP66 mL
2BufferDP35.4 mL
3StainDP10.3 mL
4StainDP20.3 mL
5Stain (staining position 2)DP56 mL
6Stain (staining position 1)DP56 mL
7MethanolDP46 mL
Reading a failure. Because each box maps to one named pump, this test localizes a dispensing problem the same way the "dark line" field case (below) localized a mechanical one — a single low/high box points at that pump's line, not a blanket "staining is off" complaint. Residual Volume Test (4 cassettes) works the same way in reverse: it checks how much is left behind after a dispense/drain cycle, catching a valve or line that isn't fully clearing.

Field case — the "dark line" smear defect

A distributor's CAL 6000 site reported intermittently poor smears: a visible dark line down the smear center, denser in cell distribution than the surrounding film, showing up on roughly 70% of slides. No foreign material was present — cells inside and outside the line were the patient's own.

  1. Observe10×/40× review confirmed the line was made of concentrated RBCs, not debris; staining and cell morphology elsewhere on the slide were normal.
  2. LocalizeThe defect tracked with the blood drop path and vanished near the tail — pointing at the aspiration-to-drying stage, not staining.
  3. Rule outSample mixing, aspiration mode (AL vs. manual), and viscosity detection were each checked and cleared.
  4. Inspect hardwareThe dispensing assembly was normal; the spreader assembly was visibly fouled with dried blood clots along its edge — built up over roughly 3 months without a maintenance intervention, and not fully removed by the automatic wash cycle.
  5. ResolveEngineer soaked and physically scraped the spreader clean; defect resolved.
Takeaway. Skipped or deferred maintenance windows are the most common root cause behind slowly-degrading smear quality — checking the maintenance log is a standard first step on any recurring smear-quality complaint, before assuming a reagent or software issue.

Maintenance menu — operator vs. service level

Menu → Service → Maintenance groups the auto-run cleaning cycles; Menu → Setup → Maintenance holds the interval settings. Frequency for each is usage-triggered (see the table earlier in this section), not purely calendar-based.

Menu itemWhat it doesTypical run time
Probe Cleanser MaintenanceCycles cleanser through the dispensing path, spreader and wash systemNot stated in the source manuals — treat as an automatic cycle, confirm completion on-screen rather than a fixed clock
Methanol Maintenance (staining cassettes)Automatically soaks the 32 staining cassettes with methanol before manual wipe-downSoak cycle duration not stated; the source does specify ~30 min for the separate manual "dip stain-waste container cap in methanol" step, and ~5 min for "dip blood-waste container cap in diluted probe cleanser" — both hand cleaning steps, not the automated cassette cycle
Screen/Analog Sensor CalibrationRecalibrates touch response and the analog level/pressure sensorsNot stated — allow 5–10 min for fan/temperature readings to stabilize afterward per the half-year inspection checklist
Honest gap. The SC-120 operation and service manuals list what each maintenance routine does and how often to run it, but do not publish exact elapsed-time figures for the automated cycles themselves — plan maintenance windows by watching the on-screen progress rather than a fixed clock, and confirm with Mindray service for site-specific timing if it needs to go into a shift schedule.

Installation, network & PC requirements

Space (by configuration)

Config 1Config 2
Each side≥ 300 mm≥ 500 mm
Above≥ 600 mm≥ 600 mm
Behind≥ 300 mm≥ 250 mm

Power & environment

100–240 V~ ±10%, 50/60 Hz, 300 VA. Environment table matches BC-6200/SC-120 (15–32 °C working / 5–40 °C operation, 30–85% / 10–90% RH).

Workstation PC — non-negotiable

Classification runs on a dedicated GPU. Vendor-specified reference card: NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1660 SUPER or better.

  • ✅ Supported: Turing generation (GTX 1660 – RTX 2080, etc.)
  • 🚫 Not supported: Ampere RTX 30-series

Only Mindray-authorized software belongs on this PC — no general-purpose use, no unmanaged USB storage; keep antivirus current.

Network — gigabit end to end

MC-80 connects to a temporary storage & distribution unit, which bridges it to the switch (no direct MC-80-to-storage-unit link); the run from MC-80 → switch and switch → workstation PC must both be gigabit cable on a gigabit switch — a 100 Mb link anywhere in that chain becomes the bottleneck for high-resolution cell images.

Upgrade path. Any existing CAL line can add MC-80 provided it already has a slide maker; if it doesn't, an SC-120 is added as part of the same upgrade. Supported lines: CAL 6000(I)/(II), CAL 7000 and CAL 8000, each with SC-120.

Consumables — just two, by design

Per the manual's own consumables list, the MC-80 uses only immersion oil and slides — everything else (stain, buffer, methanol, DI water) is consumed upstream at the SC-120, not here.

Immersion oil

Sits between the 100× oil objective and the slide during high-mag capture. Must meet index of refraction ≥1.5, stay transparent, and resist getting sticky or drying out — only Mindray-recommended brands are supported; mixing brands or mixing expired with fresh oil risks analyzer damage or bad images. Expiry date is tracked in software (Setup → Password-adjacent Oil Setup, see §03) and prompted automatically.

Slides

Consumed at the rate the SC-120 produces them, not independently — MC-80 doesn't make or stain its own slides, it only reads what SC-120 hands off through the buffer/distribution unit. Barcode label placement and print-quality requirements (§03 grading/setup) determine whether a slide is even readable, independent of oil condition.

Honest gap — no published oil-per-slide figure. Neither the MC-80 operator's manual nor the service training material states a consumption rate (e.g. mL of oil per slide, or slides per oil-bottle fill) — only the oil's physical specification and a replacement/expiry workflow are documented. Budget oil reorders by tracking the expiry-date prompt and bottle level in practice rather than a published per-slide number; if Mindray service can supply a site-specific consumption figure, it can be added here.
02

How it reads a slide

Fig. 7 — From loaded slide to a technologist-ready classification: locate → capture → extract features → classify → verify.

Locate, then capture

A low-magnification objective first scans the smear to find the region suitable for microscopic review, then photographs candidate cells at low magnification to fix their position. The stage switches to the high-magnification, oil-immersion objective and re-photographs each target cell precisely, using the position data from the low-mag pass — the reason the analyzer needs an automated oil dispenser: it must stay filled with oil between the 100× lens and slide throughout the run.

Feature extraction → classification

Each captured cell image is reduced to an eigenvector across three families of features, then handed to a classifier that assigns the closest cell type. The operator reviews and can correct every pre-classification before it's finalized — this is a triage aid, not an autonomous diagnosis.

Feature familyWhat it captures
ColorNucleus color, granule color, cytoplasm color
TextureGranule quantity/size, chromatin/parachromatin fineness, presence of nucleolus
GeometryNucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio, cell size & shape, nucleus shape

Classification criteria are anchored to WS/T246-2005 (the reference method for erythrocyte/leukocyte enumeration) — the same morphologic definitions a manual differential uses, just extracted computationally.

Mechanical path — SC-120 basket to finished review

Fig. 8 — Six subsystems a slide basket passes through between the SC-120 hand-off and the finished, reviewable image set.
03

Classification grading & QC parameters

WBC grading criteria — the 7 pre-classified types

Each type is defined by the same three eigenvector families the analyzer extracts (color / texture / geometry, per §02) — the reference criteria a tech checks against when accepting or correcting a pre-classification:

RBC morphology & platelet-estimate criteria

RBC morphology grading itself uses a separate, tunable severity scale — most recently revised in the v1.14 algorithm update to better match ICSH consensus and manual-microscopy concordance:

RBC featureGrading (pre-v1.14)Grading (ICSH, v1.14)
OvalocytesFew/1+ n/a; Mod/2+ 20–50%Mod/2+ 5–20%; Many/3+ >20%
Basophilic stippling2+ 4.0–20.0%2+ 5.0–20.0%
Stomatocyte2+ 2.0–20.0%2+ 5.0–20.0%
Target cells2+ 4.0–20.0%2+ 5.0–20.0%
Teardrop cells2+ 4.0–20.0%2+ 5.0–20.0%
Action on upgrade. After updating to v1.14, the default RBC grading thresholds must be changed manually in LabXpert — the software does not migrate them automatically.

QC threshold — smear qualification

A blood smear's non-nucleated-cell proportion depends on sample condition and smearing technique; once it exceeds a threshold the analyzer raises Unqualified QC blood smear. That threshold is adjustable per site (default 30%, configurable 0–1000%) under Morph. Setup → Others → Morph. QC Threshold Setup (service account).

LabXpert customize-tab logic (current)

  • Re-exam now includes both samples that were actually re-examined and samples that merely triggered a re-exam rule.
  • Smear now includes samples that triggered a smear rule, not only samples already smeared — except when "make smears for all samples" is enabled site-wide.
  • The Reexam Mode filter moved out from under "STAT" into its own independent condition (AND logic with the rest).

Setting up the analyzer (Menu → Setup)

ScreenWhat it configuresNotes
Setup → Para. Setup → Digital SlideScan-area center (X: 8.0–38.0 mm, Y: 8.0–18.0 mm) and scan-area size (Width 2–20 mm, Height 2–14 mm)Red rectangle on-screen previews the actual area to be scanned
Menu → Service → Simple Maint. → Oil SetupImmersion-oil expiry dateAnalyzer prompts once the set date is reached

Morphology re-exam rules — the two switches

Re-exam for PLT-Pro mode

When enabled, a sample originally run in WBC mode that turns up a user-defined number of PLT clumps (range 1–20) is automatically re-analyzed in PLT-Pro mode.

Re-exam for abnormal WBCs

When enabled for one or more of Blast cells / Plasma cells / Abnormal promyelocytes / Abnormal lymphocytes, a result inside the user-defined % range triggers a re-scan at a multiplied WBC count — a WBC multip. factor of 2 turns a 200-WBC scan into 400 WBCs on re-exam (allowed factor range 1–3).

Choosing & preparing a QC slide

Not every smear qualifies as a QC slide, and the analyzer doesn't guess — it identifies one by ID, then grades the smear itself once it's scanned:

How the analyzer recognizes a QC slide

Any slide barcode starting with the two uppercase letters "QC" is auto-identified as a QC slide on scan — print this barcode yourself if the sample doesn't already carry one. No barcode label available? Manually enter a sample ID starting with "QC" on the main-unit software screen instead, or select QC mode directly under Menu → Setup → Analysis → Sample Loading.

Case matters: lowercase "qc" is not recognized — both characters must be uppercase, whether printed on a barcode or typed as a sample ID.

Recommended QC frequency

Run one QC test per day as a baseline. Also run one outside the daily schedule:

  • After the analyzer's XYZ platform is repaired
  • After the SC-120's stain module is repaired or adjusted, on a line where the MC-80 is fed by that SC-120

A slide is only a qualified QC slide when the smear itself meets every one of these, checked before it's ever loaded:

RequirementDetail
Blood freshness & WBC levelFresh blood (prepared the same day), WBC count within normal range — recommended > 7×10⁹/L, which shortens smear-processing time and reliably yields enough countable cells
Cell countThe smear contains at least 200 nucleated cells
Non-nucleated-cell contentNon-nucleated cells (everything except identified WBC, nucleated RBC and megakaryocyte — e.g. RBCs, platelets, fragments) make up at most 30% of all cells and non-cell components found
Smear techniqueHead, body and tail are all clear — no vacuoles, no scratches
Stain qualityStaining color and color shade verified normal before use
Freedom from artifactNo obvious sediment, fragments, or smudge cells visible under the microscope
Two different cell-count floors, easy to confuse. If the analyzer locates fewer than 100 nucleated cells at all, it aborts outright and gives no result — that slide isn't usable for QC and needs replacing before you can even see a locating-accuracy score. 200 nucleated cells is the separate, higher bar a smear must clear to be considered a properly qualified QC slide in the first place (see the Preparing QC Smears requirements above) — 100 is the analyzer's hard floor to attempt scoring at all, 200 is what a good slide should deliver.

Calibrating the analyzer — QC slide cell locating

MC-80 "calibration" in routine use isn't an optical adjustment — it's a locating-accuracy correction run against a QC slide with a known cell count, done from Menu → QC:

  1. Open the QC slideSelect it from the QC slide list; the 10× cell-locating image list for that slide displays.
  2. Review each 10× imageGreen boxes = system-detected nucleated cells; blue boxes = system-detected non-nucleated cells (see the full legend below). Double-click any area to drill into the 100× sub-image.
  3. Correct what the system got wrongFound a green-boxed cell that's actually non-nucleated? Increment Found non-nucleated cells. Found a nucleated cell the system never boxed? Increment Found un-located cells.
  4. SaveTap OK — the locating results and the slide's summary recompute automatically.
  5. RepeatAcross every 10× image on the slide until the QC slide's Summary is fully validated.

Reading the cell-locating screen — what green and blue mean

Green box — nucleated cell

The cell the algorithm classifies as a nucleated cell: an identified WBC, a nucleated RBC, or a megakaryocyte. These are the cells the whole QC scheme is actually judging — the locating-accuracy score below is scored on green-boxed cells alone.

Blue box — non-nucleated cell

Everything else the field contains: mature RBCs, platelets, fragments, sediment, smudge cells. These don't count toward the ≥200-nucleated-cell qualification target — and if they crowd more than 30% of the slide's cells and components, the smear itself is graded Unqualified, regardless of how accurately the analyzer boxed the rest.

Why the distinction matters operationally: MC-80's QC test isn't re-measuring the blood count — it's confirming the analyzer's own cell-finding algorithm is still locating nucleated cells reliably, against a slide with a known, verified cell population. A smear buried in non-nucleated debris (crowded feathered edge, poor spreading technique, platelet clumps) makes that check meaningless even with a perfectly-tuned algorithm, which is exactly why the 30% non-nucleated ratio fails the smear, as a separate criterion from the locating-accuracy score itself.

Status icons on the QC screens

ScreenIconMeaning
QC slide list(blank)Smear not yet viewed
QC slide list✗ redQC failed — the analyzer located fewer than 100 nucleated cells; the result is discarded and not counted into QC at all
QC slide list✓ greenProcessed, and the system located every nucleated cell on the slide — no operator correction needed
QC slide list✓ redProcessed, but not all nucleated cells were detected — needs operator calibration (the steps above) before the slide's summary is valid
10× image list(blank)This particular 10× image hasn't been reviewed yet
10× image list✓ greenReviewed — every cell on this image was correctly detected
10× image list✓ redReviewed — some cells on this image were missed or mis-boxed

Each 10× image's analysis result displays as N1 (+N2) — N1 is the number of nucleated cells the analyzer located on that image, N2 is the number of non-nucleated cells it located alongside them. Every correction you make feeds directly into the summary formulas:

Located nucleated cellsN1 — nucleated cells the analyzer itself located, before any operator correction
Corrected nucleated cellsLocated nucleated cells − non-nucleated cells marked by the user (green boxes you reclassified as wrong)
Un-located nucleated cellsNucleated cells the analyzer missed entirely, marked by the user via "Found un-located cells"
Locating AccuracyCorrected nucleated cells / (Corrected nucleated cells + Un-located nucleated cells) × 100%
QC resultCriterion
Normal (no prompt)Locating accuracy ≥ 97.0% and non-nucleated RBC ratio ≤ 30.0%
Out of controlLocating accuracy < 97.0%
Unqualified QC blood smearNon-nucleated RBCs > 30% of the slide
QC failsFewer than 200 nucleated cells located
04

Service notes & FRU boundaries

XY assembly

Replaceable as a field-replaceable unit (FRU); its home-position sensors are separately replaceable, but the motor and grating ruler are not field-separable from the assembly.

Imaging system

Z-axis motor or microscope-body failure means replacing the entire imaging assembly — followed by re-adjusting all optical parameters and the relative positions to the recycling, loading/unloading, and temporary-storage assemblies.

Slide temporary-storage assembly

Motor/photocoupler are individually replaceable; never adjust the height of the slide-placing platform — mismatched height against the XY platform causes slides to fall.

Five working positions — temporary storage stage

  1. Home position
  2. Temporary-storage receivingSlide handed off from the turn-over/scanning assembly.
  3. Temporary-storage loadingReady to move onto the XY imaging platform.
  4. Prepare for manual loading
  5. Manual sampling positionSingle-slide mode — an operator can place one slide directly for ad-hoc review.
Barcode & orientation. The scanner reads the slide barcode and checks the print-area to determine which side carries the blood film; if the slide was loaded film-side reversed, the turn-over assembly automatically rotates it 180° before imaging. A transparent (unprinted) label area can cause a false orientation read — worth checking first if slides are coming back unimaged.
Software · Data management & autoverification

LabXpert — Laboratory Data Management Software

The rule engine sitting over every analyzer on the line: pulls results in, checks each one against a configurable validation-rule tree, and only hands a tech the samples that actually need a human look — the layer that turns raw throughput into a workable daily queue.

01

Login & architecture

Client–server, one server up to four workstations

LabXpert runs as a client–server application: one server end holds the database and rule engine, and up to 4 client workstations connect to it at once — reception/sample-entry, bench review, a pathologist's microscopy-verification seat and a supervisor/QC seat can all work the same result pool concurrently.

Two functional "ends" split the work:

  • Operation end — daily sample review, validation, re-exam handling, reporting
  • Data management end — rule configuration, QC/statistics, historical trend review, system setup

Startup & login

Two access levels gate the software: a standard operator level for daily review, and an administrator / Service-level account required to reach More → Validation Rules and enable auto validation at all. Site credentials are issued by Mindray service and site IT, not documented here.

The workflow-diagram color coding used throughout this section follows the software's own rule-tree legend: white = checking points, blue = the point currently selected, green = the pass path, orange = the fail path.

02

The validation rule tree — how a result gets auto-released

Every result that reaches LabXpert walks the same ordered checkpoint chain. A sample that clears every checkpoint is auto-validated; failing any one sends it to manual validation, a re-exam, or a microscopic exam, depending on which checkpoint stopped it and how that checkpoint is configured.

Fig. 9 — The seven-checkpoint auto-validation chain. Any checkpoint's fail path can route to manual review, a microscopic-exam condition, or a re-exam rule; clearing all seven auto-releases the result.

Checkpoint 1–3: does the result even qualify for auto-checking?

① Abnormal Sample CheckFails on aspiration-abnormal flags (Asp.Abn, RBC Agglutination?, CRP aspiration abnormal, etc.) — pass → ②, fail → Reexam Condition
② Panic Value CheckPer-parameter upper/lower critical limits, each with an optional custom message — pass → ③, fail → Reexam Condition
③ Parameter & Flag CheckTwo parts: parameter range check + flag check — pass → ④ (Normal Range Delta), fail → Abnormal Range Delta Check

④ Range Delta Check — comparing against the patient's own history

Splits into Parameter Delta Check (the current result's absolute or relative deviation from that patient's latest historical result inside a defined day window) and Flag Delta Check (comparing current vs. latest historical flags). Runs as either the Normal-Range or Abnormal-Range variant depending on which way Parameter & Flag Check resolved.

⑤ Clinical Exception — the "yes, but ignore this" rule

Built from Applicable Conditions + Exemptions + Parameter Rules + FLAG Rules. A sample meeting the conditions (and no exemption) has its listed parameter abnormality / flag ignored under "Ignore Parameter Abnormal" / "Ignore Flag" and proceeds to Normal Range Delta Check instead of Reexam Condition — the mechanism a site uses for a known, chronic abnormal result that shouldn't keep triggering review.

03

Re-exam & delta-check rules — setup reference

Manual Review Conditions vs. Reexam Condition

Manual Review Conditions

Applicable Conditions + Exemptions + Parameter Rules + FLAG Rules. Meeting the criteria (no exemption) routes the sample to Reexam Condition; everything else is Auto Validation OK.

Reexam Condition

Adds a Delta Check Rules component on top of the same Applicable Conditions / Exemptions / Parameter Rules / FLAG Rules structure — this is the checkpoint that actually decides how a triggered sample gets re-examined (see re-exam modes below).

Delta Check Rules — Day(s) / Change / Difference

SettingDefines
Day(s)The time window against which the current result is compared to that patient's latest historical result.
Change: Increase / Decrease / ChangeWhether the rule fires on a rise, a fall, or either-direction change beyond the defined limit.
Difference (#)Absolute deviation limit between the two results, per parameter.
Difference (%)Percentage deviation limit between the two results, per parameter. When both # and % are set, the sample passes if it stays within either limit.

Multiple Delta Check rules combine with AND/OR exactly like Parameter/FLAG rules elsewhere in the tree — with AND, a sample only fails Delta Check once it fails every defined rule.

Re-exam modes — what "re-exam" actually does

The specific re-exam actions available depend on which analyzers make up the sample processing line. On a CAL 6000 (BC-6200-based) line, the core set is:

Re-exam modeMeaning
Sample check (by physician)Prompts a physician-level check of whether the sample is clinically normal.
Analyzer status confirmationPrompts the operator to confirm the instrument itself is error-free and working properly before trusting the result.
Rerun in same modeRe-runs the identical test panel.
+R / +CDR / +CD / +D / +CAdds test item(s) to the original panel — e.g. original panel "CD" + a rule requiring RET ("+R") re-examines as "CDR".
CDR / RET / CR / CD / CBCReplaces the original panel entirely with the new one named by the rule.
CR/PLT-8X or CDR/PLT-8XSwitches to the PLT-8X counting method when PLT falls below a specified level (BC-6000Plus/6100Plus/6200 only).
SmearRoutes the tube to the SC-120 for a blood film — only available when an SM&S is part of the line.

Other configured sample-processing lines (BC-6800Plus, BC-7500 CRP, CAL 8000) support additional modes — dilute-and-rerun for very high WBC counts, CRP-analysis suppression, extra panel codes (CDN/CN/CDNR) — documented per-line in the LabXpert manual's re-exam-mode tables.

"Rule – First Time days." When enabled, a patient who already triggered a given re-exam rule and returns for another test within the defined number of days is not re-examined again for the same trigger — only a test after that window elapses counts as triggering the rule "for the first time" again. Configured under Other Settings.
04

Configuration groups & testing the rule tree

Configuration Group Management

Administrators can split rules by patient gender, age, department or type — so, for example, a pediatric department can run a different Panic Value Check than the general ward, without two separate rule trees. Only three checkpoints support configuration groups:

  • Panic Value Check
  • Parameter and Flag Check
  • Abnormal Range Delta Check

Default group

Built into LabXpert, accommodates every sample. Cannot be edited, disabled or deleted. A sample lands here whenever it doesn't match any custom group (or none exist).

Custom groups

Built from Applicable Conditions (gender, age, department, patient type) + Exemptions. LabXpert checks a sample against custom groups first, in order, before falling back to the default group.

Testing and adjusting the rule tree — Debug Mode

Debug Mode replays a batch of already-resulted historical samples back through the current rule tree — it's how a change gets checked against real data before it ever governs a live sample, rather than trusting that a new rule "should" behave a certain way.

  1. Open the toolMore → Validation Rules → Debug Mode opens the Rule Tree (Debug Mode) screen — the same rule-tree layout used everywhere else in this section, now driven by replayed data instead of live samples.
  2. Set the time rangeClick "Time Range", choose the historical window to pull samples from, and click OK.
  3. Start DebugClick "Start Debug" — the tree replays every sample in that window through the rules currently configured, and each checking point lights up with its pass rate in blue font, exactly like the annotated screenshot above (e.g. 77.2% clearing Parameter & Flag Check).
  4. Adjust while still in debugClick directly on a checking point whose pass rate looks wrong (too high — real problems slipping through; too low — the tech is drowning in unnecessary reviews) and edit its rule. Debug Mode lets you edit rules in place without leaving the screen.
  5. Re-run and repeatClick "Start Debug" again to replay the same historical batch against the edited rule — same data, so any change in pass rate is attributable to the rule edit, not sample drift. Repeat the click-adjust-replay loop until every checkpoint's pass rate accords with expectation.
  6. Commit or discardClick "Effect" and confirm to save the adjusted rules as the tree's live configuration — or click "Exit debug mode" to leave without saving anything, if the exercise was exploratory only.
Why this matters operationally. A rule tree tuned only in theory tends to either over-trigger (defeating the point of autoverification — the tech reviews almost everything anyway) or under-trigger (missing samples that should have been caught). Because Debug Mode replays the identical historical batch after every edit, it isolates the effect of that one rule change — the intended way to strike the balance before "Effect" makes it live, rather than tuning rules against real patients and finding out afterward. This is the same discipline behind CAL 6000's own TAT/rule setup covered in the CAL 6000 tab's LabXpert summary.
05

Reading a result — RUO parameters, i-Message, Historical Trend & Reference Results

Under Table View, a sample's result panel is built from a set of tabs the operator can customize: Report Parameters, RUO Parameters (including RUO scattergrams and reference results), i-Message, Re-Exam Results, Rule Record, and Graph (histograms, scattergrams, flags, sample workflow). The four covered here are the ones an operator reads for extra context beyond the reportable numbers themselves.

RUO Parameters — Research Use Only

A results table of research-only parameters (the same RUO parameters catalogued per-channel in the BC-6200 tab), plus their own scattergram panel — click any scattergram to enlarge it, and click the 3D icon when it appears to rotate that scattergram in 3D. These never appear on the clinical report; they're context for the reviewer only.

Flag: EThe result was edited directly by the operator
Flag: eCalculated from another parameter's result — flagged because editing that other parameter changed this one
Flag: RThe result is suspicious
Flag: ****The result has been screened (see Reference Results, next)

The RUO table's Delta column follows the same pass/fail convention used elsewhere: black font = passes Delta Check against the patient's prior result, red font = fails it. Note it has no His.1/His.2 columns of its own — LabXpert doesn't keep a historical trend for RUO parameters.

Reference Results — when a value comes back as "****"

When the system decides a parameter's result isn't reliable enough to report (e.g. certain abnormal samples' DIFF results), the Sample Report shows **** instead of a value — but the analyzer's best estimate isn't thrown away, it's parked on a separate Reference Results screen.

  1. Open RUO ParametersClick the "RUO Parameters" tab on the sample's result panel.
  2. Click "Reference Results"Opens the Reference Results dialog with the estimated value(s).
  3. Decide, then report if appropriateWeigh the reference value against historical results, microscopic exam findings, or re-exam results — click "Report Ref. Results" only once you're confident it's reliable.
Not available on automated glycohemoglobin analyzers. Reference results are also explicitly excluded from X-B QC's own sample pool (see below) — an estimate the system itself flagged as unreliable can't be allowed to feed the QC statistic meant to validate the instrument.

i-Message — clinical flags & flagging sensitivity

The i-Message tab displays the sample's clinical flags together with the sensitivity of the flagging that raised them — a window into how confidently the instrument's algorithm is calling that flag, not just that it fired.

i-Message settings are fixed by the instrument's own algorithm and cannot be edited by the operator or site administrator. Questions about a specific i-Message go to Mindray's Service Department, not to LabXpert configuration. Not available on automated glycohemoglobin analyzers.

Historical Trend — the same patient over time

Reviews a patient's result history three ways from the "Historical Trend" tab:

  • Parameter Compare — side-by-side values across past visits
  • Trend Graph — a single parameter plotted over time
  • Graph Compare — multiple parameters' trends overlaid

Also shows the trend of customized/user-defined parameters when that function is enabled site-wide. Not applicable to glycohemoglobin tests. This is the same historical-result pool that feeds the Delta Check comparisons covered earlier in this tab.

06

Daily QC — L-J QC vs. X-B QC

LabXpert supports two distinct quality-control schemes side by side, and the BC-6000-series engine behind CAL 6000 (and BC-7500 CRP) supports both:

QC typeWhat it usesWhat it's checking
L-J QC (Levey–Jennings)Assayed control material with a known mean/SD, run like a patient sample and plotted against defined limitsClassic daily control — is the instrument's output for a known sample still inside its expected range today?
X-B QCReal patient sample results — no control material consumed at allIs the instrument's long-run average on real patients still stable, using the statistical fact that a large, random patient population's red-cell indices barely drift day to day?

L-J QC's own setup and run procedure (QC files, mean/SD entry, graph review) is the standard daily-control workflow referenced as "Daily QC" in the CAL 6000 tab; the rest of this section covers X-B QC specifically, since it's the less familiar of the two.

X-B QC — what it is and when to turn it on

X-B QC is a weighted moving average analysis run on three red-cell indices — MCV, MCH and MCHC — computed from ordinary patient results instead of a control material. It's recommended once a lab's volume passes >100 samples/day: at that throughput there's enough randomized, representative patient traffic for the statistic to be meaningful, and effective use depends on that randomization holding (a skewed patient mix — e.g. a run of samples from one ward — biases the indices and defeats the point).

Fig. 10 — How one X-B QC point gets built: every valid patient result (not control material) feeds a rolling batch, and each completed batch produces one plotted point.

Setting up X-B QC rules (data management end)

Menu → QC → select the analyzer → QC Type = X-B QC:

On/OffEnable or disable the X-B program per analyzer
Samples/Batch20–200; e.g. set to 20 → the analyzer computes an X-B point the moment 20 valid samples have accumulated
Target / limitPer parameter (MCV, MCH, MCHC); none may be left blank; same units as the analyzer's own Parameter Unit setup
Sample Validity SetupUpper/lower limits for RBC, MCV, MCH, MCHC — a sample counts toward X-B only when all four fall inside their set ranges (RBC uses its linearity range; the others use their display ranges)
Restore DefaultsResets targets/limits; display mode toggles between By SD(#) and By CV%

Running it & the storage limit

Once set up, X-B QC runs automatically — no operator action starts a batch. Every time 20–200 valid samples (per Samples/Batch) have accumulated, the system computes one X-B point without prompting, reviewable afterward in the X-B QC graph or table.

The analyzer keeps up to 1000 X-B QC results. Once that cap is reached, each new point overwrites the oldest saved one — there's no separate purge step to manage.

Compiled for internal application-specialist reference from Mindray CAL 6000 / BC-6000 & 6200 / SC-120 / MC-80 & 82 training and service documentation. Verify current settings, thresholds and part numbers against the analyzer's own on-screen help and the latest OEM manuals before acting on them clinically — software versions and default thresholds change between releases.
